title: “This is a dirge for the world . . . this is saga, for a nation”: The Air India tragedy and the politics of multidirectional refusal
abstract: Despite the staggering loss of life, the 1985 Air India tragedy remains largely forgotten in the Canadian national consciousness. This article traces the evolution of literature written about the bombing of Air India Flight 182 from earlier claims for state recognition pursued by the Indo-Canadian victims’ families immediately following the tragedy to later works that employ what I term a “multidirectional politics of refusal,” seeking alternative forms of recognition and redress beyond the bounds of the state. By adopting a skepticism around recognition politics, I view this later literature through Indigenous decolonial practices of refusal, where authors work beyond the aegis of the settler state to link the Air India tragedy to other instances of transnational and (post)colonial violence to envision new forms of redress and reconciliation on their own terms.
